item.text: The BAM is present and valid in the history. I’m applying the standard interpretation: mapping quality ≥30 and SAM flag 0x2 (“mapped in a proper pair”), counting retained read alignments.

The first submitted job completed but Galaxy resolved it to the tool defaults, so it is not evidence for the answer. I’m correcting the conditional-parameter binding and will only use an output whose recorded parameters match the intended filters.

{ "history_id": "bbd44e69cb8906b5eb934ec672e4a973", "input_format": "21.01", "selected_input_format": "21.01", "tool_id": "toolshed.g2.bx.psu.edu/repos/iuc/samtools_view/samtools_view/1.22+galaxy2", "tool_inputs": { "addref_cond|addref_select": "no", "input": { "id": "f9cad7b01a47213512ccb07c74bb3ba9", "src": "hda" }, "mode|filter_config|cond_expr|select_expr": "no", "mode|filter_config|cond_region|select_region": "no", "mode|filter_config|cond_rg|select_rg": "no", "mode|filter_config|inclusive_filter": "2", "mode|filter_config|quality": 30, "mode|output_options|reads_report_type": "count", "mode|outtype": "selected_reads", "mode|subsample_config|subsampling_mode|factor": 1, "mode|subsample_config|subsampling_mode|select_subsample": "fraction" }, "validate_before_submit": true } { "action": "/tool_runner/index", "citations": true, "creator": null, "credentials": [], "description": "- reformat, filter, or subsample SAM, BAM or CRAM", "display": true, "edam_operations": [], "edam_topics": [], "enctype": "application/x-www-form-urlencoded", "errors": {}, "form_style": "regular", "has_parameters": true, "help": "

What it does

\n

Samtools view can:

\n
    \n
  1. convert between alignment formats (SAM, BAM, CRAM)
    2. \n
  2. filter and subsample alignments according to user-specified criteria
    3. \n
  3. count the reads in the input dataset or those retained after filtering\nand subsampling
    4. \n
  4. obtain just the header of the input in any supported format
    5. \n
\n

In addition, the tool has (limited) options to modify read records during conversion and/or filtering by:

\n
    \n
  • stripping them of user-specified tags
    • \n
  • collapsing backward CIGAR operations if they are specified in their CIGAR\nfields
    • \n
\n

With default settings, the tool generates a BAM dataset with the header and\nreads found in the input dataset (which can be in SAM, BAM, or CRAM format).

\n

Alignment format conversion

\n

By changing the Output format it is possible to convert an input dataset to\nanother format.\nInputs of type SAM, BAM, and CRAM are accepted and can be converted to each of these formats (alternatively alignment counts can be computed) by selecting the appropriate "Output type".

\n

The tool allows you to specify a reference sequence. This is required for SAM input with missing @SQ headers (which include sequence names, length, md5, etc) and useful (and sometimes necessary) for CRAM input and output. In the following the use of the reference sequence in the CRAM format is detailed.\nCRAM is (primarily) a reference-based compressed format, i.e. only sequence differences between aligned reads and the reference are stored. As a consequence, the reference that was used during read mapping is needed in order to interpret the alignment records (a checksum stored in the CRAM file is used to verify that only the correct reference sequence can be used). This allows for more space-efficient storage than with BAM format, but such a CRAM file is not usable without its reference.\nIt is also possible, however, to use CRAM without a reference with the disadvantage that the reference sequence gets stored then explicitely (as in SAM and BAM).

\n

The Galaxy tool currently generates only CRAM without reference sequence.

\n

For reference based CRAM input the correct refernce sequence needs to be specified.

\n

Filtering alignments

\n

If you ask for A filtered/subsampled selection of reads, the tool will allow\nyou to specify filter conditions and/or to choose a subsampling strategy, and\nthe output will contain one of the following depending on your choice under\nWhat would you like to have reported?:

\n
    \n
  • All reads retained after filtering and subsampling
    • \n
  • Reads dropped during filtering and subsampling
    • \n
\n

If instead you want to split the input reads based on your criteria and\nobtain two datasets, one with the retained and one with the dropped reads, check\nthe Produce extra dataset with dropped/retained reads? option.

\n

Filtering by regions

\n

You may specify one or more space-separated region specifications after the input filename to restrict output to only those alignments which overlap the specified region(s). Use of region specifications requires a coordinate-sorted and indexed input file (in BAM or CRAM format).

\n

Regions can be specified as: RNAME[:STARTPOS[-ENDPOS]] and all position coordinates are 1-based.

\n

When multiple regions are given, some alignments may be output multiple times if they overlap more than one of the specified regions.

\n

Examples of region specifications:

\n
\n
chr1
\n
Output all alignments mapped to the reference sequence named 'chr1' (i.e. @SQ SN:chr1).
\n
chr2:1000000
\n
The region on chr2 beginning at base position 1,000,000 and ending at the end of the chromosome.
\n
chr3:1000-2000
\n
The 1001bp region on chr3 beginning at base position 1,000 and ending at base position 2,000 (including both end positions).
\n
*
\n
Output the unmapped reads at the end of the file. (This does not include any unmapped reads placed on a reference sequence alongside their mapped mates.)
\n
.
\n
Output all alignments. (Mostly unnecessary as not specifying a region at all has the same effect.)
\n
\n

Filtering by quality

\n

This filters based on the MAPQ column of the SAM format which gives an estimate about the correct placement of the alignment. Note that aligners do not follow a consistent definition.

\n

Filtering by Tag

\n

This filter allows to select reads based on tool or user specific tags, e.g., XS:i:-18 the alignment score tag of bowtie.\nThus to filter for a specific value of the tag you need the format STR1:STR2, e.g., XS:-18 to filter reads with an aligment score of -18.\nYou can also just write STR1 without the value STR2 hence the filter selects all reads with the tag STR1, e.g., XS.

\n

Filtering by Expression

\n

Filter expressions are used as an on-the-fly checking of incoming SAM, BAM or CRAM records, discarding records that do not match the specified expression.

\n

The language used is primarily C style, but with a few differences in the precedence rules for bit operators and the inclusion of regular expression\nmatching.

\n

The operator precedence, from strongest binding to weakest, is

\n
\nGrouping        (, )             E.g. "(1+2)*3"\nValues:         literals, vars   Numbers, strings and variables\nUnary ops:      +, -, !, ~       E.g. -10 +10, !10 (not), ~5 (bit not)\nMath ops:       \\*, /, %          Multiply, division and (integer) modulo\nMath ops:       +, -             Addition / subtraction\nBit-wise:       &                Integer AND\nBit-wise        ^                Integer XOR\nBit-wise        |                Integer OR\nConditionals:   >, >=, <, <=\nEquality:       \\=\\=, !=, =~, !~   =~ and !~ match regular expressions\nBoolean:        &&, ||           Logical AND / OR\n
\n

Expressions are computed using floating point mathematics, so "10 / 4" evaluates to 2.5 rather than 2. They may be written as integers in decimal or\n"0x" plus hexadecimal, and floating point with or without exponents.However operations that require integers first do an implicit type conversion, so\n"7.9 % 5" is 2 and "7.9 & 4.1" is equivalent to "7 & 4", which is 4. Strings are always specified using double quotes. To get a double quote in a\nstring, use backslash. Similarly a double backslash is used to get a literal backslash. For example ab"c\\d is the string ab"cd.

\n

Comparison operators are evaluated as a match being 1 and a mismatch being 0, thus "(2 > 1) + (3 < 5)" evaluates as 2. All comparisons involving undefined (null) values are deemed to be false.

\n

The variables are where the file format specifics are accessed from the expression. The variables correspond to SAM fields, for example to find paired\nalignments with high mapping quality and a very large insert size, we may use the expression "mapq >= 30 && (tlen >= 100000 || tlen <= -100000)". Valid\nvariable names and their data types are:

\n
\nendpos               int            Alignment end position (1-based)\nflag                 int            Combined FLAG field\nflag.paired          int            Single bit, 0 or 1\nflag.proper_pair     int            Single bit, 0 or 2\nflag.unmap           int            Single bit, 0 or 4\nflag.munmap          int            Single bit, 0 or 8\nflag.reverse         int            Single bit, 0 or 16\nflag.mreverse        int            Single bit, 0 or 32\nflag.read1           int            Single bit, 0 or 64\nflag.read2           int            Single bit, 0 or 128\nflag.secondary       int            Single bit, 0 or 256\nflag.qcfail          int            Single bit, 0 or 512\nflag.dup             int            Single bit, 0 or 1024\nflag.supplementary   int            Single bit, 0 or 2048\nhclen                int            Number of hard-clipped bases\nlibrary              string         Library (LB header via RG)\nmapq                 int            Mapping quality\nmpos                 int            Synonym for pnext\nmrefid               int            Mate reference number (0 based)\nmrname               string         Synonym for rnext\nncigar               int            Number of cigar operations\npnext                int            Mate's alignment position (1-based)\npos                  int            Alignment position (1-based)\nqlen                 int            Alignment length: no. query bases\nqname                string         Query name\nqual                 string         Quality values (raw, 0 based)\nrefid                int            Integer reference number (0 based)\nrlen                 int            Alignment length: no. reference bases\nrname                string         Reference name\nrnext                string         Mate's reference name\nsclen                int            Number of soft-clipped bases\nseq                  string         Sequence\ntlen                 int            Template length (insert size)\n[XX]                 int / string   XX tag value\n
\n

Flags are returned either as the whole flag value or by checking for a single bit. Hence the filter expression flag.dup is equivalent to flag & 1024.

\n

"qlen" and "rlen" are measured using the CIGAR string to count the number of query (sequence) and reference bases consumed. Note "qlen" may not exactly\nmatch the length of the "seq" field if the sequence is "*".

\n

"sclen" and "hclen" are the number of soft and hard-clipped bases respectively. The formula "qlen-sclen" gives the number of sequence bases used in the\nalignment, distinguishing between global alignment and local alignment length.

\n

"endpos" is the (1-based inclusive) position of the rightmost mapped base of the read, as measured using the CIGAR string, and for mapped reads is\nequivalent to "pos+rlen-1". For unmapped reads, it is the same as "pos".

\n

Reference names may be matched either by their string forms ("rname" and "mrname") or as the Nth @SQ line (counting from zero) as stored in BAM using\n"tid" and "mtid" respectively.

\n

Auxiliary tags are described in square brackets and these expand to either integer or string as defined by the tag itself (XX:Z:string or XX:i:int).\nFor example [NM]>=10 can be used to look for alignments with many mismatches and [RG]=~"grp[ABC]-" will match the read-group string.

\n

If no comparison is used with an auxiliary tag it is taken simply to be a test for the existence of that tag. So [NM] will return any record containing\nan NM tag, even if that tag is zero (NM:i:0). In htslib <= 1.15 negating this with ![NM] gave misleading results as it was true if the tag did not exist\nor did exist but was zero. Now this is strictly does-not-exist. An explicit exists([NM]) and !exists([NM]) function has also been added to make\nthis intention clear.

\n

Similarly in htslib <= 1.15 using [NM]!=0 was true both when the tag existed and was not zero as well as when the tag did not exist. From 1.16 onwards\nall comparison operators are only true for tags that exist, so [NM]!=0 works as expected.

\n

Some simple functions are available to operate on strings. These treat the strings as arrays of bytes, permitting their length, minimum, maximum and\naverage values to be computed. These are useful for processing Quality Scores.

\n
\nlength(x)   Length of the string (excluding nul char)\nmin(x)      Minimum byte value in the string\nmax(x)      Maximum byte value in the string\navg(x)      Average byte value in the string\n
\n

Note that "avg" is a floating point value and it may be NAN for empty strings. This means that "avg(qual)" does not produce an error for records that\nhave both seq and qual of "*". NAN values will fail any conditional checks, so e.g. "avg(qual) > 20" works and will not report these records. NAN also\nfails all equality, < and > comparisons, and returns zero when given as an argument to the exists function. It can be negated with !x in which case it\nbecomes true.

\n

Functions that operate on both strings and numerics:

\n
\nexists(x)      True if the value exists (or is explicitly true).\ndefault(x,d)   Value x if it exists or d if not.\n
\n

Functions that apply only to numeric values:

\n
\nqrt(x)     Square root of x\nog(x)      Natural logarithm of x\now(x, y)   Power function, x to the power of y\nxp(x)      Base-e exponential, equivalent to pow(e,x)\n
